plan.title: How CRISPR Edits Genes: From Bacteria to Therapy
plan.description: CRISPR began as a bacterial defense against viruses, and scientists turned it into a tool that finds and cuts a chosen stretch of DNA. This video explains how Cas9 and guide RNA find a target, how the cell repairs the cut, one approved therapy, and the main ethical debate.

beats.narration: One of the most powerful tools for editing human DNA was not invented in a lab. It was found inside bacteria, where it has been fighting viruses for a very long time.
Bacteria get attacked too. Viruses called phages inject their DNA into bacterial cells and take over. Bacteria needed a defense, and many of them evolved one.
Here is the trick. When a bacterium survives an attack, it saves a snippet of the virus's DNA in its own genome. It is like a library of wanted posters.

That library is called a CRISPR array. CRISPR stands for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. Scientists named it after they saw the odd pattern, long before they understood the idea.

props.definition: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats: a pattern of repeated DNA with viral snippets stored between the repeats.

beats.narration: The pattern was first spotted in E. coli in 1987. In 2007, it was shown to defend bacteria against phages. In 2012, it was programmed to cut chosen DNA. In 2020, that earned a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

props.title: From odd repeats to Nobel Prize

events.label: Odd repeats found in E. coli DNA
Shown to defend bacteria against phages

beats.narration: So CRISPR is not a machine built from scratch. It was discovered in nature. Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier simply showed that the bacterial scissors, Cas9, could be reprogrammed.

props.text: CRISPR was not invented from scratch. It was found in nature.

beats.narration: Think of Cas9 as a pair of molecular scissors. Scissors alone cut anywhere, so they need an address. That address label is the guide RNA, which steers Cas9 to one exact spot.
beats.chapter: How Cas9 finds and cuts the right spot

beats.narration: The guide RNA is about 20 letters long. Those letters match the target DNA by base pairing, the same A-to-T and C-to-G rule that holds DNA's two strands together.

props.heading: The guide RNA
items: Matches target DNA by base pairing
A pairs with T, C pairs with G

beats.narration: Cas9 doesn't read the whole genome letter by letter. It first scans for a short tag called a PAM. Only beside a PAM does it pry the DNA open and check the guide.

props.definition: A short DNA sequence next to the target that Cas9 must find before it unwinds the DNA and checks the guide RNA.
props.example: For the common Cas9, the PAM is NGG.

beats.narration: If the guide matches, Cas9 changes shape and its two cutting domains go to work. One slices each strand, about three letters from the PAM, leaving a clean break through both strands.

steps.label: Unwind the DNA
steps.detail: Guide RNA pairs with the target

beats.narration: Now the cell must fix the break. Path one is non-homologous end joining. It is quick but sloppy, often adding or deleting letters, which usually switches the gene off.
Path two is homology-directed repair. Scientists supply a template, and the cell copies it into the gap, writing a new sequence. It is precise, but much rarer than end joining.
So far we have the cut and two ways to repair it. Next comes the real test: how this turns into an approved therapy, and the debate it raises.

beats.narration: Doctors take blood stem cells from the patient. In the lab, CRISPR edits them. Then the cells are returned to the patient's body.

steps.detail: CRISPR cuts the BCL11A control region

beats.narration: The edit switches off BCL11A's control of fetal hemoglobin. More fetal hemoglobin then makes up for the faulty adult hemoglobin that causes the disease.
But there is a catch. Casgevy was listed at 2.2 million dollars for a one-time treatment. That raises hard questions about who can actually get it.

props.label: List price of Casgevy per patient

beats.narration: The bigger debate is about whose DNA we edit. Somatic editing changes only the patient's own cells. Germline editing changes embryos, so the changes are heritable and pass to future generations.
In 2018, He Jiankui announced the birth of gene-edited babies in China. Scientists around the world condemned it, and a summit statement called clinical germline editing irresponsible.

events.label: Hong Kong summit: use remains irresponsible

accuracy.reason: The overall picture is right, but several claims are wrong or shaky: the bar chart presents the 75/25 NHEJ/HDR figure as if it were exact, the script says Casgevy 'already treats disease in one patient', and it says nothing about the FDA approval date or the second indication.

coverage.reason: Covers origin, PAM and guide RNA, NHEJ vs HDR, Casgevy with its BCL11A mechanism, and He Jiankui. It omits tracrRNA, spacer acquisition, and the CRISPR in-bacteria mechanism, and it does not say which approval came first or when.

structure.reason: The order is clean (origin, mechanism, repair, therapy, ethics) and the beat-13 transition works. Beat 13 is a filler recap and the ethics section is brief.

hook_ending.reason: The opening line is decent but fairly generic. The ending is a summary with a flawed claim, 'in one patient'.

tone.reason: Clear, beginner-friendly, and not hyped, with good analogies such as 'wanted posters' and 'address label'.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary. But the phage diagram uses an odd 'tally-1' icon, a node label is cut off ('Faulty adult hemoglobin of'), and the bar chart is built on a loose statistic.

originality.reason: The analogies are good but common, and there are few surprising specifics beyond the 1987 E. coli finding and the PAM detail.

instructions.reason: Hits every requested element at about the right length. It lacks a clear statement of the approved therapy's date or of the germline ethics beyond the 2018 case.

language.reason: Fluent and natural English, with minor awkwardness such as 'The germline line is drawn' and 'simply showed'.

defects.quote: It already treats disease in one patient.
defects.issue: Casgevy is approved for two diseases and has treated many patients. 'One patient' is wrong or at best unclear.
The 75/25 figure is a rough, context-dependent estimate from one review, but the chart presents it as a fixed fact. Real HDR rates are often much lower.

defects.quote: In late 2023, Casgevy became the first CRISPR therapy approved, first in the UK, then by the US FDA.
defects.issue: Imprecise. The UK MHRA approved it in November 2023 and the FDA in December 2023 for sickle cell disease. Beta thalassemia FDA approval came in January 2024.

defects.quote: Casgevy was listed at 2.2 million dollars
defects.issue: The US list price of $2.2M is correct, but the script does not say it is the US price.
The node label is truncated and reads as a typo on screen.

defects.quote: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier simply showed that the bacterial scissors, Cas9, could be reprogrammed.
defects.issue: No explanation of how the bacterial system works (tracrRNA, spacer acquisition). The 'simply' also undersells the work.

defects.quote: So far we have the cut and two ways to repair it.
defects.issue: A recap-style transition that adds no new content.

missing: How bacteria use the stored snippets (CRISPR RNA guiding Cas to cut returning viral DNA)
Casgevy's approval dates and the fact that it covers two diseases
Off-target edits and other safety concerns
Wider ethics: enhancement and equity beyond price
wrong_facts: 'It already treats disease in one patient' is wrong: Casgevy is approved for two diseases and many patients have been treated.
The 75% vs 25% NHEJ/HDR split is presented as a universal figure; it is a rough estimate.
Beta thalassemia FDA approval came later, in January 2024, which the script does not mention.
judge.summary: A well-organized, beginner-friendly script that covers all the requested elements, with good analogies and varied scenes. It is let down by a wrong closing claim ('one patient'), loose statistics, and thin ethics and bacterial-mechanism depth.
